tiers.title: Foundations

topics.title: Arrays & Hashing
topics.summary: Index tricks, prefix products and hash maps that turn nested loops into single passes.

topics.title: Two Pointers
topics.summary: Walk inward from both ends of a sequence to avoid quadratic scans.

topics.title: Stack
topics.summary: Last in, first out: bracket matching and monotonic stacks that find the next smaller or larger element.

topics.summary: Grow and shrink a contiguous window so every element enters and leaves it once.

components.title: Prefix Sums
components.summary_md: Running totals: `p[i]` is the sum of the first `i` elements, so the sum of any range becomes a single subtraction.

build_steps.title: Read a prefix array
build_steps.prompt_md: Before you build prefix sums, trace them. Work out what this snippet prints without running it.

payload.code:
nums = [3, -1, 4, 1]
p = [0]
for x in nums:
    p.append(p[-1] + x)
print(p[3] - p[1])
payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: `p` ends up as `[0, 3, 2, 6, 7]`, so `p[3] - p[1]` is 6 − 3 = 3 — exactly `nums[1] + nums[2]` = −1 + 4. In general `p[r] - p[l]` is the sum of `nums[l]` through `nums[r - 1]`.

hints.body_md: Write down `p` after each iteration of the loop.
`p[i]` holds the sum of the first `i` numbers, so a difference of two entries is the sum of the numbers between them.
`p[3]` is 6 and `p[1]` is 3.
It prints **3**: `p[3] - p[1]` = 6 − 3, which equals `nums[1] + nums[2]`.

build_steps.title: Build prefixSums
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `prefixSums(nums)` that returns an array `p` of length `n + 1` with `p[0] = 0` and `p[i + 1] = p[i] + nums[i]`.

You'll reuse it in **Range Sum**, so keep it general: it must handle an empty array and negative numbers. Values satisfy `|nums[i]| <= 10^4` and `nums.length <= 10^4`, so every total fits in a 32-bit integer.

tests.explain_on_fail: Negative values lower the running total.
An empty array still produces the leading 0.

hints.body_md: How is `p[i + 1]` related to `p[i]`?
Each entry is the previous entry plus one more element: build the array in a single left-to-right pass, starting from 0.

```
p = [0]
for x in nums: p.append(last(p) + x)
return p
```
The whole recurrence: `p.append(p[-1] + x)`.

```python
def prefixSums(nums):
    p = [0]
    for x in nums:
        p.append(p[-1] + x)
    return p
```

components.title: Range Sum
components.summary_md: Answer many inclusive range-sum queries in O(1) each, on top of your `prefixSums`.

build_steps.title: Spot the off-by-one
build_steps.prompt_md: An inclusive range `[l, r]` and a prefix array disagree by one index. Predict the output.

payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: `p[r + 1] - p[l]` = 10 − 2 = 8 = 5 + 0 + 3, the inclusive sum. Forgetting the `+ 1` gives `p[3] - p[1]` = 7 − 2 = 5, which silently drops `nums[3]` — the classic off-by-one.

hints.body_md: Which elements does each difference cover?
`p[i]` is the sum of the first `i` elements, so `p[b] - p[a]` covers indices `a` to `b - 1`.
Inclusive `[1, 3]` needs indices 1, 2 and 3, so it is `p[4] - p[1]`.
It prints **8 5**. Only `p[r + 1] - p[l]` includes `nums[r]`.

build_steps.title: Build rangeSum
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `rangeSum(nums, queries)`. Each query is `[l, r]` — 0-indexed, inclusive, with `l <= r` — and you return the list of their sums in order.

Call your `prefixSums` once, then answer every query with a single subtraction. With up to 10^4 queries on 10^4 numbers, re-adding each range would be far too slow.

tests.explain_on_fail: A single inclusive range in the middle.
Ranges of length one at both ends.
No queries: return an empty list.
Many queries on a long array — each must be answered in O(1).

hints.body_md: How can two entries of a prefix array give you the sum of a range?
With `p = prefixSums(nums)`, the inclusive range `[l, r]` sums to `p[r + 1] - p[l]`. Compute `p` once and reuse it for every query.

```
p = prefixSums(nums)
return [p[r + 1] - p[l] for each [l, r] in queries]
```
Mind the inclusive right end: `p[r + 1] - p[l]`, not `p[r] - p[l]`.

```python
def rangeSum(nums, queries):
    p = prefixSums(nums)
    return [p[r + 1] - p[l] for l, r in queries]
```

components.title: Is Palindrome (range)
components.summary_md: Two indices walking inward decide whether `s[lo..hi]` reads the same both ways — a reusable helper for palindrome problems.

build_steps.title: Trace the inward walk
build_steps.prompt_md: Follow the two indices as they move toward each other. Type the exact output.

payload.question: What exactly does this print?
payload.explanation_md: `"abcba"[1..3]` is `"bcb"`, a palindrome. `"abca"` fails on its first comparison (`a` vs `a` matches, then `b` vs `c` differs). For `check("ab", 1, 0)` the loop never runs because `lo > hi` — an empty range counts as a palindrome.

hints.body_md: For each call, write down which pairs of characters get compared.
The loop compares `s[lo]` with `s[hi]` and moves both inward; it stops early on a mismatch and returns `True` once the indices meet or cross.
Call 1 compares b/b. Call 2 compares a/a, then b/c. Call 3 compares nothing.
Python prints booleans as `True` / `False`, separated by spaces.
It prints **True False True**.

build_steps.title: Build isPalindrome
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `isPalindrome(s, lo, hi)` that returns whether the substring `s[lo..hi]` (inclusive) is a palindrome. Compare characters exactly — the check is case-sensitive.

An empty range (`lo > hi`) and a single character both count as palindromes. Use O(1) extra space: no reversed copies, just two indices moving inward.

tests.explain_on_fail: The whole string is a palindrome.
An inner range that is a palindrome.
An inner range of length two that is not a palindrome.
An empty range (lo > hi) counts as a palindrome.
A long range that is off by one position.

hints.body_md: Which two characters must match first, and where do you go after they do?
Two pointers: compare `s[lo]` and `s[hi]`; on a match move both inward; stop with `false` at the first mismatch and `true` once the pointers meet or cross.

```
while lo < hi:
    if s[lo] != s[hi]: return false
    lo += 1; hi -= 1
return true
```
Use `while lo < hi` — it handles the single-character and empty ranges without special cases.

components.title: Lower Bound
components.summary_md: The first index whose value is `>= target` — the workhorse behind insert positions, counting and range queries.

build_steps.title: Where does the search land?
build_steps.prompt_md: This loop searches a half-open range `[lo, hi)`. Predict where it stops.

payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: The loop keeps `mid` whenever `a[mid] >= 3`, so it converges on the **first** index holding a value `>= 3`: index 1. Ranges: `[0,5)` → mid 2 keeps left → `[0,2)` → mid 1 keeps left → `[0,1)` → mid 0 moves right → `[1,1)`.

hints.body_md: Trace `lo`, `hi` and `mid` for each iteration.
When `a[mid] >= 3` the loop keeps `mid` as a candidate (`hi = mid`); otherwise it discards everything up to `mid`.
It stops at the first index whose value is at least 3.
It prints **1** — the lower bound of 3.

build_steps.title: Build lowerBound
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `lowerBound(nums, target)` for an array sorted in non-decreasing order that may contain duplicates. Return the smallest index `i` with `nums[i] >= target`, or `nums.length` if there is none.

It must run in O(log n) — you'll build **Count in Range** on top of it.

tests.explain_on_fail: Duplicates: return the first of them.
An absent value: return the index where it would go.
Larger than everything: return the length of the array.
A long array with runs of duplicates — O(log n) is required.

hints.body_md: What should happen to the search range when `nums[mid]` is already large enough?
Search the half-open range `[lo, hi)` with `hi = len(nums)`. If `nums[mid] < target` the answer is right of `mid`; otherwise `mid` is still a candidate, so keep it.

```
lo = 0, hi = n
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) / 2
    if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid
return lo
```
Keep the candidate: `else: hi = mid` (not `mid - 1`).

components.title: Count in Range
components.summary_md: Count the values inside `[lo, hi]` of a sorted array with two `lowerBound` calls — no scanning.

build_steps.title: Two searches, one count
build_steps.prompt_md: Python's `bisect_left` is a lower bound. Predict what the difference of two lower bounds counts.

payload.code:
from bisect import bisect_left

a = [2, 4, 4, 4, 7, 9]
print(bisect_left(a, 8) - bisect_left(a, 4))
payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: The first index with a value `>= 8` is 5 (the 9); the first index with a value `>= 4` is 1. Their difference, 4, counts the values in `[4, 8)` — here 4, 4, 4 and 7.

hints.body_md: Find each lower bound separately.
`bisect_left(a, x)` is the first index whose value is `>= x`. Everything between two lower bounds lies in a half-open value range.
bisect_left(a, 8) → 5 and bisect_left(a, 4) → 1.
The difference counts values `v` with `4 <= v < 8`.
It prints **4** (the values 4, 4, 4 and 7).

build_steps.title: Build countInRange
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `countInRange(nums, lo, hi)`: how many elements `x` of the sorted array `nums` satisfy `lo <= x <= hi`?

Use your `lowerBound` twice — `lowerBound(nums, hi + 1) - lowerBound(nums, lo)` — instead of scanning. If `lo > hi` the range is empty and the answer is 0. Bounds satisfy `|lo|, |hi| <= 10^9`.

tests.explain_on_fail: Duplicates on the lower edge are all counted.
A range that contains no values.
A range covering the whole array.
A single-point range at the last value.
lo > hi describes an empty range.
A long array — two lower-bound searches, no scanning.

hints.body_md: Where does the block of values `>= lo` start, and where does the block of values `> hi` start?
With integers, "`x <= hi`" is the same as "`x < hi + 1`". So the answer is `lowerBound(nums, hi + 1) - lowerBound(nums, lo)` — two O(log n) searches.

```
if lo > hi: return 0
return lowerBound(nums, hi + 1) - lowerBound(nums, lo)
```
The upper boundary uses `hi + 1` so that values equal to `hi` are included.

components.title: Greatest Common Divisor
components.summary_md: Euclid's algorithm: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)` until the remainder reaches zero.

build_steps.title: Count the recursive calls
build_steps.prompt_md: Each call hands a smaller problem to the next one. Type the exact output.

payload.question: What exactly does this print?
payload.explanation_md: The calls are g(48, 18) → g(18, 12) → g(12, 6) → g(6, 0), which returns 6. That is 4 calls in total, so the output is `6 4`. The remainders shrink quickly — Euclid needs only O(log min(a, b)) steps.

hints.body_md: List the arguments of every call.
Each call replaces `(a, b)` with `(b, a % b)` and stops when `b` is 0.
The last call returns its `a`, and `calls` counts every call including the first.
It prints **6 4**.

build_steps.title: Build greatestCommonDivisor
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `greatestCommonDivisor(a, b)` for non-negative integers that are not both zero, using Euclid's rule `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)` with `gcd(a, 0) = a`.

Recursion is natural here and its depth is only logarithmic. Inputs go up to 10^12, so use 64-bit integers.

tests.explain_on_fail: The same pair with the arguments swapped.
Large powers of two times a small factor — needs 64-bit integers.

hints.body_md: If `d` divides both `a` and `b`, what else must it divide?
Any common divisor of `a` and `b` also divides `a mod b`, so `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`. The second argument shrinks every step until it is 0.

```
gcd(a, b):
    if b == 0: return a
    return gcd(b, a mod b)
```
The recursive step: `return greatestCommonDivisor(b, a % b)`.

components.title: Least Common Multiple
components.summary_md: `lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b` — divide first so the intermediate value stays small.

build_steps.title: Multiples from divisors
build_steps.prompt_md: Predict both values before you build the component.

payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: `gcd(21, 6)` is 3, so `lcm(21, 6)` = 21 // 3 × 6 = 42 (not 21 × 6 = 126). For `lcm(0, 5)`: `gcd(0, 5)` is 5 and 0 // 5 × 5 = 0 — the only multiple of 0 is 0.

hints.body_md: Compute each gcd first.
`lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b`: the product divided by the shared factor.
It prints **42 0**.

build_steps.title: Build leastCommonMultiple
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `leastCommonMultiple(a, b)` for non-negative integers, using your `greatestCommonDivisor`. Return 0 if either input is 0.

Divide before multiplying — `a / gcd(a, b) * b` — so the intermediate value never exceeds the result. Inputs go up to 10^6 and results up to 10^12, which needs a 64-bit integer.

tests.explain_on_fail: Two large primes: the result needs 64 bits.
The common factor must be divided out exactly once.

hints.body_md: How does the product `a × b` relate to the lcm?
`a × b = gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b)`, so `lcm = a / gcd(a, b) * b`. Dividing first keeps the numbers small.

```
if a == 0 or b == 0: return 0
return a / greatestCommonDivisor(a, b) * b
```
Use integer division: `a // greatestCommonDivisor(a, b) * b` (in Python).

components.title: Merge Sorted Arrays
components.summary_md: Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array in a single linear pass — the heart of merge sort.

build_steps.title: Where did the tail go?
build_steps.prompt_md: This merge loop has a subtle bug. Predict what it prints.

payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: The loop stops as soon as **either** array runs out. Once `9` is taken, `a` is exhausted and the loop ends — so `10` and `11`, the rest of `b`, are never copied. A correct merge appends whatever remains of both arrays after the loop.

hints.body_md: Trace `i`, `j` and `out` step by step. When does the loop condition become false?
The condition requires both arrays to have elements left, so the leftover elements of the other array are never added.
out grows 1, 2, 4, 4, 9 — then i == 3 and the loop stops with j == 2.
`b[2]` and `b[3]` (10 and 11) are still unread when the loop exits.
It prints **[1, 2, 4, 4, 9]** — the tail `10, 11` is lost.

build_steps.title: Build mergeSorted
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `mergeSorted(a, b)`. Both inputs are sorted in non-decreasing order and either may be empty; return a new sorted array containing every element of both.

Walk both arrays with two indices in one linear pass — don't concatenate and sort — and remember to copy whatever is left over. **Merge Sort** will call this.

tests.explain_on_fail: Interleaved values with a tie; the longer tail must be copied.
b both starts before and ends after a.
Every element of a comes before every element of b.
Two long arrays — one linear pass.

hints.body_md: Which element belongs at the very front of the result?
The smallest remaining element is always at the front of `a` or the front of `b`. Take the smaller one, advance that index, and repeat; when one array runs out, append the rest of the other.

```
i = j = 0, out = []
while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
    take the smaller of a[i], b[j] (prefer a on ties)
append a[i:] and b[j:]
```
Don't forget the leftovers after the loop: `out.extend(a[i:]); out.extend(b[j:])`.

```python
def mergeSorted(a, b):
    out = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            out.append(a[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(a[i:])
    out.extend(b[j:])
    return out
```

components.title: Merge Sort
components.summary_md: Split in half, sort each half recursively, and combine the halves with `mergeSorted` — O(n log n) on every input.

build_steps.title: How many merges?
build_steps.prompt_md: Count how often the combine step runs when sorting eight elements.

payload.code:
merges = 0

def sort(a):
    global merges
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = sort(a[:mid]), sort(a[mid:])
    merges += 1
    return sorted(left + right)  # stand-in for a real merge

sort([5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 7, 3, 6])
print(merges)
payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: Every call on two or more elements merges once. Splitting 8 → 4 + 4 → 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 gives 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 merges; in general a full split of `n` elements performs `n − 1` merges.

hints.body_md: Draw the recursion tree for 8 elements.
Only calls on arrays of length ≥ 2 reach the merge line; single elements return immediately.
Level sizes: one call on 8, two on 4, four on 2.
It prints **7** — `n − 1` merges for `n = 8`.

build_steps.title: Build mergeSort
build_steps.prompt_md:
Write `mergeSort(nums)` that returns a new array with the values of `nums` in non-decreasing order.

Split the array in half, sort each half recursively, and combine the two sorted halves with your `mergeSorted`. Don't call a built-in sort — the point is to see O(n log n) emerge from the recursion.

tests.explain_on_fail: A shuffled array of eight values.
Two elements in the wrong order.
Reverse sorted — merge sort stays O(n log n) whatever the order.

hints.body_md: If both halves of the array were already sorted, what would you do?
Divide and conquer: sort the left half and the right half recursively, then merge them with `mergeSorted`. Arrays of length 0 or 1 are already sorted — that is the base case.

```
mergeSort(nums):
    if len(nums) <= 1: return copy of nums
    mid = len(nums) / 2
    return mergeSorted(mergeSort(nums[:mid]), mergeSort(nums[mid:]))
```
The combine step: `return mergeSorted(mergeSort(nums[:mid]), mergeSort(nums[mid:]))`.

components.title: BFS Distances
components.summary_md: Breadth-first search from one source in an unweighted graph: the first time a node is reached, it is reached along a shortest path.

build_steps.title: Visited too late
build_steps.prompt_md: This BFS marks nodes as visited when they are **dequeued**. Count how many times something is pushed onto the queue.

payload.question: What exactly does this print?
payload.explanation_md: Node 3 is reachable from both 1 and 2. Because nodes are only marked when dequeued, 3 is still "unseen" when node 2 is processed, so it is pushed a second time: 0, 1, 2, 3, 3 — five pushes. Marking nodes when you **enqueue** them guarantees each node enters the queue once.

hints.body_md: Track the queue contents and the `seen` set after each dequeue.
A node is only added to `seen` when it leaves the queue, so it can be pushed again by another neighbour before that happens.
Pushes: 0 (initial), then 1 and 2 from node 0, then 3 from node 1, then 3 again from node 2.
When node 2 is processed, node 3 is waiting in the queue but not yet in `seen`.
It prints **5**.

build_steps.title: Build bfsDistances
build_steps.prompt_md:
Nodes are labelled `0 .. n-1` and each `[u, v]` in `edges` is an **undirected** edge (self-loops and repeated edges may appear). Return an array `dist` where `dist[v]` is the fewest edges on any path from `src` to `v`, or `-1` if `v` cannot be reached; `dist[src]` is 0.

Use a queue and mark nodes as visited when you **enqueue** them. **Shortest Path Length** will reuse this.

tests.explain_on_fail: Two equally short routes lead back to the source.
A single node and no edges.
Two components; the source is in the smaller one.
A cycle: distances grow in both directions.
A 30 × 30 grid graph explored from a corner.

hints.body_md: In what order should nodes be explored so that closer nodes are always finished first?
Breadth-first search: a FIFO queue processes nodes in order of distance. The first time you discover a node, its distance is final — record it and enqueue it right away.

```
build adjacency lists (both directions)
dist = [-1] * n; dist[src] = 0; queue = [src]
while queue:
    u = pop front
    for v in adj[u]:
        if dist[v] == -1: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1; push v
return dist
```
Use `dist[v] == -1` as the "not visited yet" test and set it before enqueueing: `dist[v] = dist[u] + 1; queue.append(v)`.

```python
from collections import deque

def bfsDistances(n, edges, src):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
    dist = [-1] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    queue = deque([src])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] == -1:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                queue.append(v)
    return dist
```

components.title: Shortest Path Length
components.summary_md: One BFS answers "how many hops from src to dst?" — reuse `bfsDistances` and read off a single entry.

build_steps.title: First found is shortest
build_steps.prompt_md: BFS may explore a long route first. Predict the distance it records for node 3.

payload.question: What does this print?
payload.explanation_md: The queue processes nodes level by level: 0, then 1 and 4, then 2 and 3. Node 3 is first discovered from node 4 at distance 2, before the longer route 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 gets there. In an unweighted graph, the first discovery is always along a shortest path.

hints.body_md: Write down the queue after each step.
BFS finishes every node at distance d before it looks at any node at distance d + 1.
Node 3 is discovered while processing node 4, whose distance is 1.
It prints **2**.

build_steps.title: Build shortestPathLen
build_steps.prompt_md:
Return the number of edges on a shortest path between `src` and `dst` in the same undirected graph format as **BFS Distances**, or `-1` if they are not connected. `src == dst` needs zero edges.

Reuse your `bfsDistances` — this should take a line or two.

tests.explain_on_fail: The only path runs through every node.
An extra edge creates an equally short second route.
The source is the destination: zero edges.
Source and destination lie in different components.
The opposite side of a cycle.
A 30 × 30 grid: corner to opposite corner.

hints.body_md: You already have a function that computes the distance to *every* node.
Run `bfsDistances(n, edges, src)` and return the entry for `dst`; it is already `-1` when `dst` is unreachable.

```
return bfsDistances(n, edges, src)[dst]
```
The whole body: `return bfsDistances(n, edges, src)[dst]`.

```python
def shortestPathLen(n, edges, src, dst):
    return bfsDistances(n, edges, src)[dst]
```
